articles.title: Where Can I Find Compatible Replacement Molds for an Existing PET Injection Molding System?
articles.summary: Compatible replacement molds for an existing PET injection molding system come from three places: the machine maker, independent preform mold makers and conversion specialists that build from your existing parts. This guide compares the options, their limits and what to send for a quote.

heroImage.alt: Multi-cavity PET preform mold lifted by an overhead crane between the platens of an injection molding machine

detailImage.alt: Replacement preform mold parts — cores, cavity inserts, neck rings and lock rings — on a granite inspection table

sections.heading: Where can I find compatible replacement molds for an existing PET injection molding system?
paragraphs: You can find compatible replacement molds from three kinds of suppliers: the machine maker's own tooling and service division, independent PET preform mold makers that build to your machine's interface, and conversion specialists that manufacture new parts from your existing mold components. The right choice depends on whether you need an identical copy, a modified preform or a complete new mold, and on what your service contracts allow.

A compatible replacement mold is a preform mold, or a set of mold parts, made to fit an existing injection molding machine's platens, hot runner interface, cooling circuits and take-out system without modifying the machine itself.

Disclosure: this article is published by LIHE Precision. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. We are an independent mold maker, not a machine OEM, and we describe machine makers only by what their own websites state.
list: Machine OEM tooling: suits plants that want one supplier for machine and mold, or whose service agreement specifies OEM tooling.
Independent mold maker: suits plants that want a new mold, a different cavity count, a new neck finish or a lighter preform on a machine they already own.
Conversion from existing parts: suits plants that need worn cores, cavities, neck rings or lock rings replaced so they match the current mold exactly.

sections.heading: What “compatible” has to cover
paragraphs: In injection molding the mold is only one part of a system. A replacement mold must work with every machine-side element it touches, and each of the points below should be checked against the real machine, not only against a catalogue model name.
list: Machine interface: platen mounting pattern, locating ring, clamp stroke and mold shut height.
Hot runner interface: nozzle pitch, gate design, manifold layout, and heater and thermocouple wiring to the existing controller.
Cooling: water circuit layout, connectors and flow capacity for cores, cavities and neck rings.
Post-mold handling: cavity pitch and geometry that match the robot take-out plate and its cooling tubes.
Preform specification: neck finish (for example PCO 1881, 1716, 2925 or 38mm), wall thickness, weight and length.
Cavitation: the same cavity count as before, or a change that the machine's shot size and clamp force can support.

Pricing: whether prices are published or quoted.

articles.title: Compression vs Injection Molding for Plastic Closures: A Practical Comparison
articles.summary: Plastic caps can be made by compression molding or by injection molding. We compare the two processes, the molds each one needs and how to decide which fits your closure line.

heroImage.alt: Compression molding tooling for plastic caps — punches, dies and cores — next to finished bottle caps

detailImage.alt: Multi-cavity closure injection mold core plate with polished cap cores

sections.heading: What is compression molding for closures?
paragraphs: In closure compression molding, each cavity receives an exact-weight pellet of melted resin, which is then formed into a cap under high pressure. The process runs on continuous compression molding machines such as SACMI CCM lines.

Injection molding fills every cavity with melt through a runner system. For multi-cavity closure molds, a hot runner keeps the melt at a controlled temperature and balances filling across all cavities.

sections.heading: Key terms
list: Compression molding: a process in which a measured dose of molten plastic is placed in an open mold cavity and shaped by closing the mold under pressure.
Continuous compression molding (CCM): a rotary compression machine, such as a SACMI CCM line, that cuts, places and forms doses in a continuous cycle.
Injection molding: a process in which molten plastic is injected through a runner system into a closed mold, held under pressure, cooled and ejected.
Hot runner: a heated manifold and nozzle system that keeps the plastic molten on its way to each cavity, so there is no cold runner to cool, cut off or regrind.
Tamper-evident (TE) band: a ring at the bottom of the cap that breaks or separates on first opening, showing the consumer that the bottle has been opened.
Tethered cap: a cap that stays attached to the bottle after opening, as required for many beverage containers in the EU.
One-piece and two-piece caps: a one-piece cap seals with features molded into the cap itself, while a two-piece cap combines a shell with a separate liner or seal.
Cavitation: the number of cavities in a mold, which together with the cycle time sets the output of the line.

sections.heading: Why compression molding runs faster
paragraphs: Because compression molding works at a lower processing temperature, the cap needs less cooling time. Shorter cooling means shorter cycles, higher output and lower energy use per cap than conventional injection.

sections.heading: How each process works
paragraphs: The sequences below describe the general process for each technology. Machine makers set the actual process parameters, and they depend on the resin, the cap design and the machine.
steps: Compression: an extruder melts the resin continuously and delivers it to the dosing system.
Compression: a cutter separates a dose of exact weight and places it into the open cavity.
Compression: the punch and die close and form the cap under high pressure, including the thread and the tamper-evident band.
Compression: the cap cools in the closed tooling and is then ejected; cutting or folding of the tamper-evident band can be done as a separate downstream step.
list: Injection: the resin is melted in the barrel of the injection molding machine.
Injection: the melt is injected through a hot runner into all cavities of the mold at the same time.
Injection: holding pressure compensates for shrinkage while the caps cool against the cooled cores and cavities.
Injection: the mold opens and the caps are ejected, for example by stripping or unscrewing them from the cores.

Injection strength: runs on mainstream closure injection molding machines, which many converters already own.
Injection strength: a hot runner balances filling across many cavities; LIHE closure injection molds range from 12 to 72 cavities.
Injection limit: the higher melt temperature means more heat must be removed from every cap, which is why cooling design matters for cycle time.

sections.heading: Neck finishes and applications
list: Neck finishes: 26mm, 28mm, 2925, 3025, 38mm and custom specifications.
Applications: water, juice and tea drinks, edible oil, condiments and soy sauce, cosmetics, health-care products, pharmaceuticals and food packaging.
EU tethered caps: both compression and injection closure molds can be built for tethered cap designs.

sections.heading: EU tethered caps and what they mean for tooling
paragraphs: Directive (EU) 2019/904 on single-use plastics requires caps and lids of plastic beverage containers of up to 3 litres to stay attached to the container during use, with the requirement applying from July 2024. For closure producers this means the cap design includes a tether that links the cap to the tamper-evident band or neck ring after opening.

A tethered cap can be produced by compression molding or by injection molding. The tether is usually formed by the cap geometry and by cutting or slitting the band, so the cavity, core and band details must be designed together with the downstream equipment. LIHE builds both compression molds and closure injection molds for EU tethered cap designs.

sections.heading: Common closure defects and what usually causes them
list: Flash on the cap edge or thread: worn or damaged shut-off surfaces, or excessive pressure or material for the cavity.
Short shots or incomplete threads: too little material in the cavity, blocked venting, or uneven filling between cavities.
Cap weight or dimension variation between cavities: hot runner imbalance in injection molds, or dose weight variation in compression lines.
Ovality of the cap: insufficient or uneven cooling before ejection.
TE band that breaks too early or does not break on opening: band geometry, bridge dimensions or slitting are out of specification.
Leaking caps: worn sealing features on cores or punches, or a mismatch between the cap and the bottle neck finish.

sections.heading: Maintenance considerations
list: Compression tooling: inspect punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts at fixed intervals and replace worn parts before they affect cap dimensions.
Injection molds: check hot runner nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals, because these parts control balanced filling across all cavities.
Both: keep cooling channels clean, since scale reduces heat removal and lengthens the cycle.
Both: keep venting clear and protect sealing surfaces and polished cores during cleaning.
Hold spare sets of high-wear parts for your main cap formats, so a single damaged part does not stop a multi-cavity mold.

sections.heading: How to decide
steps: Start from your machines: compression tooling is built for SACMI CCM lines, while injection molds run on closure injection molding machines.
Look at volume and energy cost: high-volume lines benefit most from the shorter cycles and lower energy per cap of compression molding.
Confirm the cap design: one-piece or two-piece, tamper-evident band, tethered cap and neck finish.
For an existing line, send your current parts or drawings; replacement compression tooling can be made from existing parts.
Set the output target and cavitation, then compare the number of cavities your machine can carry with the volume you need.
Ask for inspection reports and plan spare parts for high-wear components before the mold goes into production.

faq.answer: Yes. Replacement compression tooling — punches, dies, cores, cooling inserts and wear parts — can be made from your existing parts and is machined and inspected in-house.

faq.answer: Not automatically. Compression molding offers shorter cycles and lower energy per cap, but it requires a compression line such as a SACMI CCM machine. The better choice depends on the machines you own, your volume and your cap design; an exact tooling price requires a quotation.

articles.title: What Are My Options If I Need a Drop-in Replacement Hot Runner for a PET Preform Mold?
articles.summary: If you need a drop-in replacement hot runner for a PET preform mold, you can refurbish the existing system, buy new from the original hot runner maker, order a compatible system from an independent supplier, or replace only the worn components. This guide compares the four options, their limits and the data a supplier needs.

heroImage.alt: Hot runner manifold plate for a multi-cavity PET preform mold with rows of nozzles and bundled wiring on a workbench

detailImage.alt: Hot runner nozzle tips, valve pins and coil heaters arranged on a steel tray

sections.heading: What are my options if I need a drop-in replacement hot runner for a PET preform mold?
paragraphs: You have four options: refurbish the hot runner you already have, buy a new system from the original hot runner maker, order a compatible system from an independent supplier, or replace only the worn components such as nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals. The right option depends on the condition of the manifold and plates, how long the mold must keep running and how much downtime you can accept.

A drop-in replacement hot runner is a hot runner system — manifold, nozzles, heaters and valve gates — built to fit the existing mold plates, gate positions, wiring and temperature controller of a PET preform mold, so it can be installed without redesigning the mold.

Disclosure: this article is published by LIHE Precision. LIHE Precision (Foshan Lihe Precision Machinery Co.,Ltd.) is a manufacturer of PET preform molds, blow molds, closure and compression molds, hot runner systems and mold components for the beverage and packaging industry, with manufacturing in Foshan, China. We are one of the independent suppliers described below, not a machine OEM.
list: Refurbishment: best when the manifold and plates are sound and the problems are wear, leaks or heater failures.
New from the original hot runner maker: best when you want the same design, documentation and service channel as before.
Compatible system from an independent supplier: best when you want a new system for an existing mold at a separately quoted price, or the original design is no longer supported.
Component replacement only: best when a few nozzles or heaters fail and the rest of the system performs well.

sections.heading: What “drop-in” must match
paragraphs: A hot runner keeps PET molten from the machine nozzle to each gate. In a preform mold it sits between the machine and the cavity plate, so a replacement has to match several interfaces at once. Each item below should be confirmed with drawings or measurements from the actual mold.
list: Plate dimensions and stack height, so the mold closes and clamps exactly as before.
Nozzle pitch and gate positions, which must line up with every cavity.
Gate type: most preform hot runners use valve gates, where a valve pin opens and closes each gate.
Valve pin actuation and air supply, matched to the mold's existing pneumatic circuit.
Heater zones, wattage and thermocouple type, matched to the existing controller and its cable connectors.
Melt channel design, so the melt is balanced across all cavities and residence time stays short; PET is sensitive to heat history, and uneven melt temperature shows up as variation between cavities.

paragraphs: We compare the four options on the same dimensions. LIHE values come from LIHE's published product and company pages. For hot runner makers we only repeat what their official websites list and cite those sites in the references. Values that depend on a quote are marked as quoted, not estimated.

Fit risk: how likely the result is to need adjustment at installation.

sections.heading: How to choose: a decision path
list: Is the manifold cracked, or does it leak at the manifold rather than at the nozzles? Plan for a new system, either from the original maker or from a compatible supplier.
Is the manifold sound but several nozzles, heaters or seals fail? Refurbish the existing hot runner.
Is only one zone or nozzle affected? Replace that component and record the failure so patterns become visible.
Is the original design no longer supported, or do you want a second source? Ask an independent supplier for a compatible system and send full drawings.

Are you also changing cavity count, neck finish or preform weight? Treat it as a mold project, not a drop-in replacement; LIHE lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1g to 2g, and retrofits cost 25%–40% of a new mold price.

sections.heading: Price and total cost of ownership
paragraphs: Hot runner prices are always quoted per project, because they depend on cavity count, pitch, gate type and the state of the existing system. Compare options on total cost, not on purchase price alone.
list: Cavity count: a 144-cavity system has many more nozzles, heaters and valve pins than a small one.
Downtime: a leaking hot runner stops the whole mold, so the cost of lost production often exceeds the cost of parts.
Leak risk: a written leakage guarantee, such as LIHE's 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on its Husky Ultra-type design, moves part of that risk to the supplier.
Mold life: there is little value in a new hot runner on a mold near the end of its life; LIHE tooling is built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms.
Spare parts: keep critical spares — nozzle tips, heaters, valve pins — on site; LIHE quotes replacement parts at 4 weeks.

sections.heading: How to request a drop-in replacement hot runner
steps: Record the current system: maker, model, number of drops, nozzle pitch, gate type and the mold's cavity count.
Collect the hot runner and mold plate drawings; if none exist, ask the supplier about measuring the existing system.
Note the controller make, number of zones, heater wattage and thermocouple type.
Describe the failure history: which zones leak or fail, how often, and after how many cycles.
Ask the supplier which option it recommends — refurbishment, new system or parts — and why, with a written scope and guarantee.
Plan installation and start-up with the supplier's technical team, and agree a preventive maintenance schedule.

articles.title: Hot Fill vs Cold Fill PET Blow Molds: How to Choose the Right Mold
articles.summary: Hot fill and cold fill PET blow molds are built for different filling temperatures. This guide compares how each mold works, which beverages each one suits and what to specify when you order a new mold set.

heroImage.alt: Opened PET blow mold halves showing a bottle cavity, lit warm and cool to contrast hot fill and cold fill

detailImage.alt: Clear PET bottles on a conveyor after stretch blow molding, including a hot fill bottle with vacuum panels

sections.heading: What is the difference between a hot fill and a cold fill blow mold?
paragraphs: A cold fill blow mold produces PET bottles that are filled at ambient temperature, such as still water, carbonated soft drinks (CSD), juice and dairy. A hot fill (heat-set) blow mold produces bottles that are filled hot, at around 85–95°C, for products such as juice, tea drinks and isotonic beverages.

The difference matters because standard PET bottles start to deform above about 60°C. A hot fill mold uses heated mold walls to crystallize and stabilize the bottle during blowing, so it keeps its shape when hot product goes in.

sections.heading: Key terms used in this guide
list: Cold fill: the beverage is filled at ambient or chilled temperature, so the bottle never has to withstand hot product.
Hot fill: the beverage is filled hot, at about 85–95°C, so the heat of the product helps keep the bottle and closure free of microorganisms.
Heat-set: a blow molding process in which the bottle is formed against heated mold walls, which raises crystallinity and relieves stretch-induced stress so the bottle tolerates hot product.
Vacuum panels: flexible areas in the bottle wall or base that move inward as the hot product cools and contracts, so the rest of the bottle keeps its shape.
Aseptic filling: the product and the bottle are sterilized separately and filled in a sterile environment, usually at ambient temperature.
Two-step (reheat) blow molding: preforms are injection molded first, then reheated and stretch blow molded on a separate machine such as a SIDEL, KRONES or KHS blower.
One-step blow molding: the preform is injection molded and blown on the same machine, as on SIPA, ASB or AOKI systems.

sections.heading: Key numbers at a glance
list: Hot fill temperature: about 85–95°C.
Deformation point of standard (non-heat-set) PET bottles: about 60°C.
Cold fill: ambient-temperature filling, no heat-set process required.

sections.heading: How a hot fill mold keeps the bottle stable
paragraphs: In a heat-set mold the shells carry hot oil instead of only cooling water. The heated cavity walls crystallize the PET during blowing, which raises the temperature the bottle can tolerate. As the hot product cools in the closed bottle, the internal pressure drops; vacuum panels in the bottle design absorb that pressure change so the bottle does not collapse or panel unevenly.
Because the mold runs at elevated temperature for long periods, the mold material and cavity finish are chosen for long-term operation under heat.

sections.heading: How the heat-set blowing cycle works
paragraphs: The heat-set cycle follows the same basic stretch blow molding sequence as cold fill, with extra steps to stabilize the PET. The exact temperatures and timings are set by the machine maker and the bottle design, so treat the sequence below as a description, not as process settings.
steps: The preform is reheated above the glass transition temperature of PET so that it can be stretched.
A stretch rod pushes the preform down while blowing air expands it against the cavity walls of the mold shells and base mold.
Instead of cooling the bottle at once, the heated mold walls hold the PET at an elevated temperature, which raises crystallinity and relaxes stress from stretching.
The bottle is cooled before it leaves the mold, typically by flushing air through its interior, so it keeps the shape of the cavity when released.
On the filling line the bottle is filled hot, capped and cooled; the vacuum panels absorb the volume change as the product contracts.

sections.heading: Where a cold fill mold saves cost
paragraphs: Cold fill bottles do not need the heat-set structure, so the design work focuses on using less PET. Bottle geometry and base design are matched to the preform for even wall thickness at reduced bottle weight, and integrated cooling channels keep bottle quality stable at production speed. For producers with many bottle formats, a split-type quick-change mold lets you swap only the cavity inserts and base instead of the whole mold set.

sections.heading: Aseptic filling: the third option
paragraphs: Aseptic lines sterilize the product and the container separately and fill in a sterile zone, usually at ambient temperature. Because the bottle does not see hot product, it does not need a heat-set structure, and its design is closer to a cold fill bottle. LIHE builds blow molds for cold fill, hot fill and aseptic applications, so the filling method of the line, not the beverage alone, decides which mold you need.
list: Choose cold fill for water, CSD and other products that do not need heat treatment in the bottle.
Choose hot fill when the product is filled hot at about 85–95°C, for example many juices, tea drinks and isotonic beverages.
Choose an aseptic mold when your filling line uses aseptic technology for sensitive products filled at ambient temperature.

sections.heading: Common problems and what usually causes them
list: Paneling or ovalization after hot filling: the bottle design, vacuum panels or heat-set conditions do not match the filling temperature.
Shrinkage and volume loss in hot fill bottles: insufficient heat-set stabilization, so the bottle relaxes when hot product goes in.
Deformed or loose neck finish on hot fill bottles: the neck finish is not suited to hot product; some hot fill bottles use a crystallized (opaque white) neck finish for this reason.
Uneven wall thickness in cold fill bottles: the preform design and the bottle geometry are not matched, or the preform heating profile is not balanced.
Pearlescence (white haze) in the bottle wall: the PET has been stretched too far or at too low a temperature.
Incomplete details, such as soft logos or a poorly formed base: blocked or insufficient venting in the mold shells or base mold.
Stress cracking in carbonated bottle bases: base geometry and material distribution do not suit the internal pressure of the product.

sections.heading: Maintenance considerations for hot fill and cold fill molds
list: Cold fill molds: keep cooling water clean and treated, because scale or corrosion in the channels reduces cooling and makes bottle quality drift.
Hot fill molds: check hot oil connections, seals and hoses regularly, and keep separate temperature control of the body and base working as designed.
Both types: clean venting slots and holes, because blocked vents cause incomplete forming and visible marks on the bottle.
Both types: protect polished cavity surfaces during cleaning and storage; scratches transfer directly to the bottle surface.
Keep spare base molds and cavity inserts for high-volume formats, so a damaged part does not stop the line.
Record mold temperature settings and bottle quality checks for each format, so a mold can be restarted quickly after a changeover.

sections.heading: What is the best way to increase cavitation on an existing preform mold?
paragraphs: Cavitation is the number of cavities in a mold, which means the number of preforms produced in each shot. The best way to increase it depends first on the injection molding machine: if clamp force, shot capacity, platen space, post-mold cooling and auxiliary equipment can handle more cavities, the usual route is a new mold base and a new, balanced hot runner, reusing stack components (cores, cavities, neck rings) where the preform design stays the same.

Adding cavities inside the original mold plates is rarely possible, because the plates, cooling layout and hot runner manifold are designed for a fixed pitch and cavity count. If the machine itself is the limit, more cavities on the same machine will not work, and the decision becomes a question of a larger machine or a second line.

list: LIHE preform molds are built from 2 to 160 cavities.
LIHE mold bases are made for preform molds up to 160 cavities, machined on Mazak, Makino and Haas, ground on Okamoto and verified on a Zeiss CMM.
LIHE valve gate hot runners are available for up to 144 preform cavities, with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on the Husky Ultra-type design.
Published lead times: pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks, replacement parts 4 weeks.
Over 12,000 cavities are produced per year at LIHE.

sections.heading: Check the machine and line capacity first
list: Clamp force: more cavities increase the projected area and the clamp force needed to keep the mold closed.
Shot size and plasticizing rate: the extruder must melt more PET per cycle without raising melt temperature and AA.
Platen and tie-bar space: the larger mold must fit between the tie bars and on the platens, including the hot runner and water connections.
Mold height and opening stroke: confirm the new stack height and the stroke needed for ejection.
Post-mold cooling and take-out plate: the robot or take-out plate must have matching positions for every new cavity.
Hot runner controller: one zone per drop plus manifold zones; the controller may need more zones.
Chiller, dryer and material handling: water flow, cooling capacity and dried-resin throughput rise with cavitation.
Downstream capacity: blow molders, conveyors and packing must absorb the extra preforms.

sections.heading: What to prepare before you request a proposal
list: Machine brand, model, clamp force, tie-bar spacing, platen drawing and screw size.
The current mold drawings, cavity count, pitch and the hot runner make and model.
The preform drawing, weight and neck finish, and whether any of these should change.
The condition of the existing stack components: shot count, wear, and recent inspection results.
Take-out plate and post-mold cooling details, and the hot runner controller zone count.
Target output per hour and the current cycle time, so that the new cavitation can be compared with the alternatives.

sections.heading: Step-by-step: upgrading cavitation
steps: Audit the machine and line capacity against the target cavitation and decide whether the current machine can run it.
Inspect the existing stack components and decide which can be reused; measure critical dimensions on a CMM.
Choose the upgrade option: new mold base and hot runner around reused parts, or a complete new mold.
Design the new cavity layout and pitch, the cooling circuits and a naturally balanced hot runner, and check them with flow analysis.
Confirm interfaces: take-out plate positions, hot runner controller zones, water manifolds and machine connections.
Manufacture the mold base and hot runner, refurbish reused stack parts and inspect every component.
Assemble and test the mold, then run a trial to check weight balance, preform quality and cycle time on every cavity.
Install and start up on the production machine, and validate the process with per-cavity data before full production.

sections.heading: Hot runner and balance considerations
list: Every additional cavity adds a drop to the manifold; flow paths to each drop must have the same length and pressure drop for equal fill.
A naturally balanced layout is preferred to one that relies on temperature tuning to compensate for unequal flow paths.
More cavities mean more heater zones and thermocouples, so plan the controller and wiring as part of the upgrade.
Valve gates give consistent gate quality across many cavities; check that valve actuation is synchronised across the whole layout.
A larger manifold holds more melt; keep residence time in mind, because longer residence raises AA.

list: Pitch: the center-to-center distance between cavities, which limits how many cavities fit on a plate.
Projected area: the area of all cavities and runners seen from the clamp direction, which drives required clamp force.
Stack components: the core, cavity, neck rings and gate insert that form one preform.
Naturally balanced hot runner: a manifold in which every drop has the same flow length and geometry.
Coordinate measuring machine (CMM): a device that measures geometry with a probe to verify parts against the drawing.

faq.answer: Rarely. The plates, cooling layout and manifold are designed for a fixed pitch and cavity count. In most cases a new mold base and hot runner are needed, and stack parts in good condition can be reused.

articles.title: We're Moving a PET Bottle Line to 100% rPET—What Mold and Hot Runner Changes Do We Need?
articles.summary: A practical guide for plant engineers converting a PET preform and bottle line to 100% rPET: which preform mold, hot runner and cooling changes to check, how to run the conversion step by step, and how to fix the defects that typically appear.

heroImage.alt: Multi-cavity PET preform injection mold in a machine with a bin of recycled PET flakes in the foreground

detailImage.alt: Polished hot runner manifold with valve gate nozzles and heater bands on a workshop bench

sections.heading: What mold and hot runner changes does a 100% rPET line need?
paragraphs: rPET (recycled polyethylene terephthalate) is PET recovered from used bottles and reprocessed into food-grade flakes or pellets that can replace virgin resin. In most conversions the preform mold steel and cavity layout can stay as they are; the changes concentrate on the hot runner (nozzle tips, valve pins, seals, heaters and temperature balance), on venting and cooling in the mold, and on drying and material handling in front of the machine.

The reason is that 100% rPET behaves less uniformly than virgin PET: intrinsic viscosity (IV) varies from lot to lot, the material is more sensitive to moisture and heat history, and it carries more volatiles and fine contaminants. A mold and hot runner that run well on virgin resin can show black specks, haze, gate defects and weight variation once rPET reaches 100%.

sections.heading: Key numbers for planning an rPET conversion
list: Preform molds can be specified from 2 to 160 cavities; the conversion approach is the same, but every extra cavity adds a hot runner drop to balance.
LIHE valve gate hot runners are available for up to 144 preform cavities, with a 3-year leakage-proof guarantee on the Husky Ultra-type design.
Optimized mold cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s, which helps recover cycle time if rPET forces a cooler, slower process.
Lightweighting proposals reduce preform weight by 1 g to 2 g; with rPET, confirm stretch behaviour before taking weight out.
Published lead times: replacement parts 4 weeks, pilot molds 20 days, standard PET molds 8 weeks.

sections.heading: What changes when the resin becomes 100% rPET
list: IV variation: recycled flake and pellet lots differ in IV, so melt viscosity, fill balance and preform weight move between lots.
Moisture sensitivity: wet PET hydrolyses in the barrel and hot runner, which lowers IV and weakens the finished bottle.
Heat history: rPET has already been melted at least once, so extra residence time in the manifold raises acetaldehyde (AA) and yellowing.
Volatiles and fines: more gas and dust in the melt means faster vent fouling and deposits on cavity and core surfaces.
Contaminants: gels, specks and foreign particles that pass the recycler's filtration can partially block nozzle tips and gates.
Colour: rPET usually has a slight tint; haze or yellowness from the process is easier to see than with virgin resin.

sections.heading: What to prepare before you convert
list: The rPET specification from your supplier: IV range, moisture on delivery, contamination limits and the food-contact approval of the recycling process (for example an FDA no-objection letter in the U.S.).
Baseline data from the current virgin line: cycle time, reject rate per cavity, preform weight per cavity, AA level and IV drop from pellet to preform.
A capacity check of the dryer and material conveying system, because rPET flake has a different bulk density and drying response than virgin pellets.
A condition audit of the hot runner: heater and thermocouple readings per zone, nozzle tip and valve pin wear, seal condition and any leakage history.
A condition audit of the mold: vent depth, cooling water flow and temperature difference per circuit, scale in channels and wear on neck rings and locking tapers.
The preform and bottle drawings, plus blow molding results, so that any change to wall thickness or weight can be checked on the blow molder.

steps: Record a full baseline on virgin PET so every later change can be compared against real numbers.
Agree the rPET specification with your supplier and test incoming lots for IV and moisture before they reach the dryer.
Confirm dryer residence time and dew point capacity for the rPET throughput, following the resin supplier's drying data.

sections.heading: Related concepts
list: Intrinsic viscosity (IV): a measure of PET molecular weight; it falls when PET is degraded by moisture or heat.
Acetaldehyde (AA): a by-product of thermal degradation of PET that can affect the taste of water and sensitive drinks.
Hydrolysis: the reaction of molten PET with water, the main reason undried material loses IV.
Valve gate hot runner: a hot runner in which a pin opens and closes each gate mechanically, giving cleaner gates than thermal gates.
Crystallinity: ordered regions in PET that appear as white haze in a preform when cooling is too slow.

faq.question: Do we need a new preform mold to run 100% rPET?
faq.answer: Usually not. The cavity layout and steel can normally stay. The work focuses on the hot runner, venting, cooling and drying. A new mold is only needed if the existing mold is worn out or the preform design itself must change.

faq.question: Which hot runner parts wear fastest with rPET?
faq.answer: Nozzle tips, valve pins and seals are the first parts to check, followed by heaters and thermocouples. Contaminants and deposits in rPET expose wear and weak zones faster than virgin resin.

faq.question: Why do we see more black specks after the switch?
faq.answer: rPET has a longer heat history, so melt that stays in manifold dead spots degrades sooner. Cleaning or refurbishing the manifold, reducing residence time and confirming filtration usually fix it.

faq.question: Will 100% rPET make our cycle time longer?
faq.answer: It can, if the process has to run cooler or slower to control AA and haze. Optimized cooling, which can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s, is one way to recover part of that time.

sections.heading: What is a tooling conversion service?
paragraphs: Tooling conversion means producing replacement parts and performance upgrades for a PET preform mold you already own. Working from your existing Husky, SACMI or Otto parts, LIHE delivers matching tooling parts that you can fit to your existing mold.

Conversion goes beyond one-to-one replacement. It is also used for neck finish conversions and lightweighting projects, which reduce resin consumption, and for improving cooling efficiency to shorten cycle times.

sections.heading: Key terms
list: Mold stack: the set of parts that forms one preform, typically the core, cavity, gate insert and neck rings, held in place in the mold plates.
Neck rings: split inserts that form the neck finish (thread, support ring and tamper-evident bead) and open to release the preform.
Neck finish: the standardized thread and sealing geometry of the bottle opening, such as PCO 1881, PCO 1810, 2925 or 38mm; it must match the closure.
Lightweighting: reducing preform weight, usually by optimizing the neck finish or wall thickness, while keeping the bottle performance required.
Hot runner: the heated manifold and nozzles that deliver molten PET to every cavity; worn nozzle tips, valve pins, heaters and seals affect filling and preform quality.
CPK: a process capability index that compares the spread of a measured dimension with its tolerance; a higher value means more consistent parts.
CMM: a coordinate measuring machine that measures part geometry in three dimensions against the drawing.

articles.title: Our PET Preform Mold Is Running Slow and Causing Defects—What Troubleshooting Steps Should We Take?
articles.summary: A step-by-step troubleshooting guide for PET preform molds that have lost cycle time and started producing defects: what data to collect, how to isolate cooling, hot runner and mechanical causes, and a defect table with checks and fixes.

heroImage.alt: Gloved hands inspecting a clear PET container beside an opened multi-cavity preform mold on a workbench

detailImage.alt: Row of transparent PET preforms on a lit inspection table with a magnifier and calipers

sections.heading: What should you do when a preform mold runs slow and makes defects?
paragraphs: Preform mold troubleshooting is a structured process of isolating whether a cycle-time or quality problem comes from the material, the machine, the hot runner, the mold cooling or the mold mechanics. Start by collecting data per cavity, then check drying, cooling water, hot runner zones and wear parts in that order, because most slow, defect-prone molds have a cooling or hot runner fault that operators have compensated for by extending the cycle.

Cycle time refers to the full time of one injection, hold, cooling, mold opening, ejection and closing sequence. When cooling becomes less effective, the usual reaction is to add cooling time to stop haze or ovality, so the slow cycle and the defects are often the same problem.

sections.heading: Key numbers to keep in mind
list: Capability target: LIHE tooling consistently achieves CPK ≥ 1.33, a common benchmark for a capable process.
Defect benchmark: operational defect rates as low as 0.0064% on LIHE tooling.
Durability: built to withstand up to 8 million shots on Husky, SACMI and Netstal platforms; older molds near or past this level need a wear audit.
Cooling: optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.
Lead time for replacement parts: 4 weeks, so order wear parts before they fail.

sections.heading: Why preform molds slow down
list: Scale and corrosion in cooling channels reduce heat transfer, so operators extend cooling time to avoid haze and deformed preforms.
Low water flow or a high supply temperature from the chiller has the same effect across the whole mold.
Failed heaters or thermocouples in the hot runner leave cold drops; the cavity is shut off or the process is slowed to fill it.
Worn gate inserts, nozzle tips and valve pins cause gate defects that are often treated with longer hold or cooling time.
Worn neck rings, locking tapers and cores cause flash and wall eccentricity, which can force slower injection.
Wet or poorly dried resin lowers IV and increases defects, which some plants try to manage with process changes instead of fixing drying.
Blocked vents trap air and volatiles, causing short shots and burn marks that slow down setup and restarts.

sections.heading: What to prepare before troubleshooting
list: Cycle time history from the machine, ideally from when the mold was new or last refurbished.
Reject rate and defect type per cavity, with physical samples labelled by cavity number.
Preform weight per cavity from several shots, to see imbalance in the hot runner.
Cooling water records: supply temperature, flow per circuit and temperature difference between inlet and outlet.
Hot runner controller readings: set point, actual temperature and output percentage per zone.
Dryer records: drying time, dew point and material throughput.
Maintenance history: last refurbishment, parts replaced, total shot count.

sections.heading: Step-by-step troubleshooting procedure
steps: Define the problem with numbers: current cycle time versus the original, defect types and the affected cavities.
Separate cavity-specific problems from whole-mold problems; a few bad cavities point to local causes, a uniform problem points to material, water or process.
Check material drying and IV drop before touching the mold, since wet resin produces many of the same defects as mold faults.
Measure water flow and temperature difference on every cooling circuit; descale or clean channels that show low flow.
Review hot runner zones; repair heaters and thermocouples that run at abnormal output or cannot reach set point.
Inspect gates, nozzle tips and valve pins of the affected cavities and replace worn parts.
Inspect cores, cavities, neck rings and locking tapers for wear, damage and misalignment; clean and measure the vents.
Measure critical stack components, preferably on a CMM, and compare them with the drawing.
Restart with a documented process, reduce cooling time step by step and confirm preform quality at each step.
Record the root cause, the fix and the new cycle time, and update the preventive maintenance plan.

list: Use cavity-level statistical process control; CPK is a useful single number to show if a cavity or the whole mold is drifting.
Never compensate a mechanical fault with process settings for long; it hides the root cause and costs cycle time every shift.
Water quality matters as much as temperature; treated water slows down scale build-up in narrow core cooling channels.
Consider a cooling optimization when refurbishing; LIHE's optimized cooling can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.

sections.heading: Related concepts
list: Intrinsic viscosity (IV): an indicator of PET molecular weight that drops with moisture and heat damage.
Acetaldehyde (AA): a degradation product of PET that rises with melt temperature and residence time.
Stack components: the core, cavity, neck rings and gate insert that form one preform.
Hot runner balance: equal melt temperature and flow to every drop, which is needed for equal preform weight.
Process capability index (CPK): a measure of how well a process stays within its specification limits.

faq.question: What is the most common reason a preform mold gets slower over time?
faq.answer: Reduced cooling efficiency, usually from scale or blocked cooling channels or poor chiller performance. Operators extend cooling time to avoid haze and ovality, so the cycle slowly gets longer.

faq.question: How do we tell a mold problem from a material problem?
faq.answer: Look at the defect pattern by cavity. Defects in only some cavities point to local mold or hot runner causes. Defects in all cavities at once point to material, drying, water supply or process settings.

faq.question: Should we replace parts or refurbish the whole mold?
faq.answer: Replace parts when wear is limited to a few cavities. Consider a complete refurbishment when many cavities show wear, the shot count is high, or the mold no longer reaches its original cycle time after repairs.

faq.answer: Yes, if cooling is the limiting factor. Cleaning channels restores lost performance, and an optimized cooling design can reduce neck cooling time by up to 0.5 s.

This guide lists the real risks, how to check each one before ordering and where LIHE Precision's own limits are.

sections.heading: How risky is it to use non-OEM molds for PET bottle production?
paragraphs: The risk is moderate and controllable. It depends less on the OEM or non-OEM label than on whether the mold maker can prove three things: that the mold fits your machine, that it holds the preform or bottle dimensions consistently, and that it can support you when something goes wrong. A supplier that can show capability data, inspection reports and a working service team is a low-risk choice; one that cannot is a high-risk choice, whatever its price.
A non-OEM mold is a preform, blow or closure mold made by a company other than the original equipment manufacturer of the production machine, built to run on that machine without modifying it.
Disclosure: this article is published by LIHE Precision, which makes non-OEM molds. We describe machine makers only by what their own websites state and we list our own limitations below.

sections.heading: Where the risk actually comes from
list: Interface mismatch: the mold mounts but does not match the hot runner, cooling circuits or take-out plate, which delays start-up.
Dimensional variation: neck finish, wall thickness or preform weight drift between cavities, which shows up as closure leaks, uneven bottle walls or rejects on the blow molder.
Wear life: steel, heat treatment or surface finish that do not last the planned number of shots.
Hot runner leaks: poor sealing or balance that stops the mold and causes cleaning downtime.
Documentation: no drawings, inspection reports or spare-part lists, which makes later repairs slow.
Support: no one available to help with installation, start-up or troubleshooting.
Contracts: some machine service agreements may set conditions on third-party tooling; only your agreement and the OEM can confirm this.
